blocks.text: IF FACEBOOK BROUGHT YOU HERE, HERE’S THE CONTINUATION YOU’VE BEEN WAITING FOR. ENJOY! 👇 I asked Morrison to call the facility again while I reached for my phone. Michael’s doctors had been with him that evening, and I needed to hear one of their voices tell me there had been a mistake. No one could give me that reassurance.

Liam asked to call Emma’s hospital. Morrison arranged it, and I watched Liam’s face as the nurse explained that Emma had been transferred to a private research facility two hours earlier. He lowered the phone without speaking.

I knew then that whatever had happened to Michael wasn’t an isolated kidnapping. Someone had found two families desperate for the same rare treatment and used that desperation to get close to us. Liam looked at me as though I might know how to fix it, and I hated that I didn’t.

I asked Morrison to make finding both patients the priority. Liam was still a suspect in the bombing, and I understood that the police couldn’t simply hand him over to me. After further questioning and arrangements with investigators, he was permitted to leave under conditions that required him to remain available.

We rode together to my research complex in an armored car. I called Dr. Sarah Chen, the genetic specialist overseeing Michael’s care, and asked her to meet us there. Liam sat with his hands clasped so tightly that his knuckles had turned pale.

“Tell me about Emma,” I said. He told me she liked tea parties and had recently persuaded the nurses to help her organize one for other children on the ward. Even when walking exhausted her, she’d insisted on serving everyone else first.

I told him about Michael, who was twenty-one when our parents died ten years earlier. He had kept me company through the years when I was learning to run the family business, and he’d started a reading program for fellow patients after his diagnosis. Talking about him made the empty seat beside me feel unbearable.

Sarah met us in the laboratory, where police were already examining Michael’s treatment area. She had reviewed access logs and found evidence that someone had copied research files and altered treatment records over several months. The changes involved compounds our team had never approved.

She also found records linked to twelve other children with Hoffman-Larsson syndrome who had disappeared from hospitals during the previous six months. The files suggested that families had been offered experimental treatment through intermediaries. We passed everything to the investigators.
Liam stared at the names on Sarah’s screen. “Twelve children,” he said. “And Emma makes thirteen.”
“Michael makes fourteen,” I answered. The number made me sit down.

Sarah had traced references to restricted compounds through a company called Meridian Bios Systems, associated with a warehouse in Queens. She cautioned that the records didn’t prove the children were there. Still, it was the first location anyone had found that connected the altered research to the missing patients.

I wanted to go straight to Queens, and Liam wanted to come with me. Sarah argued that we should let the police secure the site, and she was right. We shared the address and the records, but when we heard that officers were still coordinating their response, neither Liam nor I could bear waiting at the lab.

We went to the area with my security driver, keeping our distance from the warehouse. It looked abandoned from the street, though lights and working ventilation suggested otherwise. Liam noticed a service area similar to those he’d cleaned during his night shifts.

He had spent years working in hospitals and office buildings, listening to maintenance staff discuss problems while people around him barely noticed he was there. That knowledge helped him recognize the building’s layout. I was ashamed to realize how often I had walked past workers like him without learning their names.

From a position near the building, we could see a security station through a window. Monitors displayed rooms on lower floors, and Liam suddenly gripped my sleeve. One screen showed a small figure with strawberry-blonde hair lying in a medical bed.

Another monitor showed a young man whose shoulders and face I knew immediately. Michael was lying still beneath a sheet, connected to medical equipment. I had spent three years studying every change in his appearance, and there was no mistaking him.

We contacted Morrison with what we’d seen. He told us to withdraw and wait for officers, but a movement near the security station made Liam fear that the children might be moved again. Before I could stop him, he approached the entrance and demanded to see his daughter.

The guards focused on him while I found a service stairwell. I knew entering was reckless, and I knew I was putting myself in danger. But I also knew Michael was somewhere below me, and I couldn’t make myself turn back.

The lower level held rows of patient rooms and equipment. I saw children in beds, some awake and some asleep, and I understood that the records Sarah had found were connected to real people. I did not touch the machines or medications; I looked for Michael and Emma and tried to remember every room number.
Emma was asleep beneath a blanket, looking painfully small. I found Michael a few rooms away, and when I said his name, he opened his eyes and whispered, “Eevee.”

He told me the staff had been giving him unfamiliar injections and taking samples. He was weak but conscious, and he worried about the other children. I promised I would tell the authorities exactly where they were.
I returned to Emma and brought her to Michael’s room. She stirred and asked for her daddy. “He’s here,” I told her. “He came for you.”

We made it back toward the checkpoint, where Liam saw his daughter and reached for her with both hands. “Hey, baby girl,” he whispered. Emma put her cheek against his shoulder and said she’d known he would come.

An alarm sounded before we could get clear. Outside, unmarked vehicles were arriving, and men moved around the building in a way that made it impossible to know who was there to help. We found an exit through a service area and tried to get away without separating.

The next minutes were confused and terrifying. Armed pursuers appeared, shots struck nearby concrete, and we fled through a storm-drain access with Liam carrying Emma while I helped Michael keep moving.

Water rose around our ankles and then our knees as we followed the tunnel toward an old subway connection. Michael struggled to breathe, Emma shivered against her father’s chest, and voices behind us made it clear we hadn’t lost everyone following us.

We reached a maintenance ladder and climbed into an abandoned subway passage, then emerged near an active platform among early commuters. I was relieved to see ordinary people carrying coffee and checking their phones, but our family still needed medical help and protection.

I called Senator Patricia Hawthorne, the woman who had become Michael’s and my guardian after our parents’ deaths. She had a secure home in the Hudson Valley and promised to contact federal law enforcement immediately. We headed toward Grand Central to meet a trusted family driver.

Emma looked at me while we waited and asked, “Are you my daddy’s girlfriend?” Liam and I exchanged a startled glance. He said I was very special to him, and I answered that he was special to me too, though neither of us knew what that meant yet.

Part 3 James, our longtime driver, collected us in an armored sedan. Two dark SUVs appeared to follow us as we left Manhattan, and he took a different route through traffic until they were no longer behind us. I kept one hand on Michael’s shoulder and watched Liam hold Emma close.

At Patricia’s Hudson Valley home, a medical team examined both patients while we told her what we’d seen. She contacted federal authorities, and investigators began securing the evidence and organizing a rescue operation for the children still at Meridian.

I remember sitting beside Liam as Emma finally slept. He was too tired to speak, and I couldn’t stop watching her breathe. The doctors said both she and Michael needed careful monitoring after the unauthorized treatments, but neither appeared to have suffered immediate permanent injury.

Federal agents searched the Queens facility and rescued the twelve remaining children. Their families were notified, and the children received medical care. I felt relief for those parents, followed by anger that someone had convinced them the only way to save their children was to surrender control of their treatment.

Investigators traced the operation through shell companies, research suppliers, and people working inside legitimate medical institutions. They identified a network of investors and pharmaceutical interests seeking to profit from neurological treatments developed through unlawful human experimentation.

Dr. Marcus Vaughn, a former researcher who had lost his medical license years earlier, emerged as the central organizer. Federal agents arrested him at a private airfield in New Jersey while he was trying to leave with research data and cryptocurrency valued at about forty million dollars.

The investigation eventually identified at least forty-seven people across twelve states connected to the scheme. Agents also located operations in California and Texas, preserving records and protecting additional patients before more evidence could disappear.

I gave a detailed statement about everything I’d seen inside the warehouse. Liam did the same, including his part in the attempted bombing. The investigators made clear that warning me did not erase his earlier involvement, and he cooperated with the case while his own legal situation was reviewed.

That mattered to me. I didn’t want to pretend he had never made a terrible decision, or that a frightened parent could do anything without consequence. But I also knew that when he understood the danger, he had chosen to stop it.

Michael and Emma’s underlying illness remained serious. A pediatric specialist, Dr. Martinez, explained that their immediate condition was improving after the unauthorized treatment stopped, but there was no established cure for Hoffman-Larsson syndrome. We would need to keep looking for legitimate options.

Patricia asked me what I planned to do with the research facility once Michael was stable. I told her I didn’t know. For years, every project had been measured against one question: Would it help my brother?
“What if it could help other families too?” she asked.

We began discussing a properly governed foundation for rare pediatric diseases, with independent medical oversight and research conducted under established rules. Liam had spent months navigating hospital bills, schedules, and unanswered questions, and I wanted families like his to have a voice in what we built.

I suggested calling it the Drake-Cross Foundation for Pediatric Research. Liam looked embarrassed when I said his name aloud, and I told him that his experience mattered just as much as my funding. We agreed that any work involving patients would need consent, safeguards, and a willingness to admit uncertainty.

Somewhere in those conversations, our friendship became something neither of us could easily explain. We’d met during a catastrophe, and I knew that wasn’t the same as knowing how we’d live together afterward. But I wanted the chance to find out.

Emma noticed before either of us had said much. She asked Liam whether he intended to marry me, then looked at me as though the answer ought to be obvious. We laughed, but later Liam and I talked seriously about what a shared life would mean for her, for Michael, and for us.

He showed me a simple gold ring that had belonged to his mother, who died when he was twelve. He said he’d kept it because she’d asked him to give it to the woman he wanted to marry. When he asked whether I would accept it, I said yes.

We decided on a small wedding at Patricia’s home. Michael stood beside Liam, Emma stayed close to me, and a few people who had helped us through the crisis witnessed our vows. Patricia arranged for the ceremony to be conducted legally, and I remember Liam’s hand shaking when he placed the ring on my finger.

Afterward, Emma asked whether we were a family now. I told her we were learning to be one, and that the promise we’d made was to keep showing up for one another. She seemed satisfied with that answer and asked when she could have cake.

Six months later, our foundation was operating with Dr. Sarah Chen helping oversee its research. Liam had left his janitorial job to become director of family services, where he worked with parents who knew what it felt like to sit beside a hospital bed without answers.

Sarah presented a proposal for supervised clinical trials based on the foundation’s early findings. She explained that the preliminary data suggested possible benefits, but the treatments were still experimental and needed proper review. She asked whether Michael and Emma might consider participating after the necessary approvals.

I spoke with Liam, Michael, and Emma before agreeing to consider enrollment. Emma wanted to know whether it would hurt, and we answered as carefully as we could. She asked us to stay beside her during treatment, and we promised we would.

Final The supervised trials began after the required approvals, and over the following months Michael and Emma showed improvements in strength and daily functioning. The researchers reported promising results, but they continued to monitor risks and made no claim that the disease had been cured.

Emma returned to ordinary childhood routines, including school, games, and chasing fireflies in the yard. Michael began writing the novel he’d talked about for years, and eventually finished a manuscript he was proud enough to submit to publishers.

Liam sometimes sat with Emma at bedtime while she asked questions about the people who had hurt the children. Once she said she hoped they understood that sick kids should feel safe in hospitals. He told her he hoped so too, and reminded her that grown-ups were working to keep other families safe.

The criminal cases took longer than our rescue. Vaughn was convicted and later died in federal prison eighteen months after his conviction, while other participants faced sentences for their roles. The network was dismantled, and the foundation’s legitimate research eventually benefited thousands of families.

As our first wedding anniversary approached, Liam and I sat on the porch of our home in Westchester watching Emma and Michael play outside. He asked whether I regretted how quickly our lives had changed, and I told him my only regret was that we hadn’t met sooner.

He drew me closer while Emma laughed at something Michael said. I still ran a company, and he still knew how to fix things I couldn’t, but neither of us measured our family by titles or bank accounts anymore.
